---
title: "Standardized measures"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dpi = 96)
```

A standardized measure summarises the fitted model as one evaluation of
each provider: how its outcomes compare with those expected under a
national norm. `standardize()` computes the measures of every model class
in the same form; `test_measure()` tests a measure against a reference
value on its own scale.

## Indirect and direct standardization

Let $O_i$ be provider $i$'s observed total (its outcomes summed, or its
number of events) and $E_i(a)$ the total its own patients would have had
at a provider with effect $a$, given the fitted risk-factor coefficients:
a sum of fitted means for a logistic or linear model, the fitted intensity
accumulated over the periods at risk for a Cox model. The norm
$\hat\mu$ is the median of the provider effects by default (robust to the
outlying providers that are the object of the exercise), or their
size-weighted mean, or a number.

**Indirect** standardization compares the provider's observed total with
the total its own patients would have had at the norm:

$$\mathrm{ISR}_i = \frac{O_i}{E_i(\hat\mu)}, \qquad
\mathrm{ISD}_i = \frac{O_i - E_i(\hat\mu)}{m_i} .$$

The question is "did this provider's patients do better or worse than they
would have at a typical provider?". The quantity tested is the provider
effect itself.

**Direct** standardization applies the provider's fitted effect to the
patients of every provider, and compares the result with the norm applied
to the same patients:

$$\mathrm{DSR}_i = \frac{\sum_{i'} E_{i'}(\hat\gamma_i)}{\sum_{i'} E_{i'}(\hat\mu)}, \qquad
\mathrm{DSD}_i = \frac{\sum_{i'} E_{i'}(\hat\gamma_i) - \sum_{i'} E_{i'}(\hat\mu)}{n} .$$

The numerator divided by the total number of observations is the
**directly standardized rate** of provider $i$: the rate the whole
population would have had at this provider. Two providers' direct rates
are comparable without further case-mix adjustment, which is why several
measures report them. The estimand is then a population-average rate, a
smooth monotone function of the provider effect, and testing it needs the
transport described below.

Ratios are used for counts and times to event, differences for continuous
outcomes. A ratio above 1 or a difference above 0 means more of the
outcome than expected.

## `standardize()`

```{r}
library(pprof)
d <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 60, provider_size = c(15, 60), seed = 7)
pd <- pp_data(d, y = "y", x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider",
              patient = "patient", message = FALSE)
fit <- fit_logistic_fe(pd)
ind <- standardize(fit, type = "indirect")
head(ind)
dir <- standardize(fit, type = "direct")
head(dir)
```

The columns: `observed`, `expected`, `ratio`, `rate` (the ratio times the
population rate, on the 0-1 scale) and `variance_expected` (indirect:
$\sum N p_0(1 - p_0)$, the variance of the expected count under the
null; direct: the delta-method numerator). Attributes record the type, the
null value, the population size and rate.

* `null`: `"median"` (default), `"mean"` (weighted by rows) or a number.
* `n_pop`: the denominator of the rates; by default the number of trials
  among the fitted rows.
* `providers`: a subset to report; the norm and the expectations always
  use every fitted row.

### Confidence limits of the measures

Limits of the ratio and the rate are mapped from limits of the provider
effect, obtained by inverting one of the tests (`ci = "exact"`, `"score"`,
`"wald"` or `"robust_wald"`):

```{r}
head(standardize(fit, type = "indirect", level = 0.95, ci = "score"))
```

### The standard error of a direct rate

A direct rate is a function of one provider effect, so any standard error
of $\hat\gamma_i$ transports to it by the delta method: `se_rate =
numer_se / n_pop * se(gamma_i)`, with $\hat\beta$ held fixed. Give the
standard errors of a Wald test as `gamma_se`:

```{r}
tst <- test(fit, statistic = "wald", variance = "robust")
dir <- standardize(fit, type = "direct", gamma_se = stats::setNames(tst$se, tst$provider))
head(dir[, c("provider", "rate", "se_rate")])
```

## Testing a direct measure: `test_measure()`

The measures that report direct rates test the rate against the national
rate on the rate scale (or on the logit scale), with the transported
standard error. `test_measure()` is the measure-level z test
$z_i = [g(M_i) - g(M_{ref})] / [g'(M_i)\, SE_i]$ with $g$ the identity,
the logit or the log:

```{r}
mt <- test_measure(estimate = dir$rate, se = dir$se_rate,
                   reference = attr(dir, "population_rate"), transform = "logit",
                   providers = dir$provider)
head(mt)
table(mt$flag)
```

Its null distribution is $N(\text{location}, \text{scale}^2)$: the
theoretical null by default, a known inflation such as `scale = 1.8`, or
an empirical null through `null_model` (see
[Reference distributions](null.html)). The intervals invert the test and
are mapped back to the measure scale.

## Continuous outcomes

For a linear fit the measures are differences: indirect $(O_i -
E_i)/m_i$, direct relative to the population mean of the effects.

```{r}
dc <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 40, type = "continuous", seed = 8)
pc <- pp_data(dc, y = "y", x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider",
              patient = "patient", message = FALSE)
head(standardize(fit_linear_fe(pc)))
```

## Survival outcomes

For a Cox fit the indirect measure is the observed-to-expected ratio
$O_j / E_j$ with $E_j$ the events expected at the national baseline for
the provider's own records, together with the person-time (the grouping
variable of the survival measures' empirical null); the direct measure is
$E^{(j)} / O$ with $E^{(j)}$ the events expected if every patient had
provider $j$'s own baseline, computed from the risk-set sums.

```{r}
s <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 60, provider_size = c(15, 60), type = "survival", seed = 9)
ps <- pp_data(s, x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider", patient = "patient",
              time = "stop", start = "start", event = "event", cutoff = 0, message = FALSE)
cox <- fit_cox(ps)
head(standardize(cox))
head(standardize(cox, type = "direct"))
```

The ratios of a Cox fit are tested by `test(cox)`, which treats the
observed count as Poisson with the expected count as its mean (see
[Tests of provider effects](testing.html)).

## An arbitrary standard population

`direct_expectation()` evaluates the direct numerator for any provider
effects and any standard population (a linear predictor and trials per
row), for instance a national population from another year:

```{r}
direct_expectation(gamma = coef(fit)$gamma[1:3], linear_predictor = fit$linear_predictor)
```

## Reference

He K (2019). Indirect and direct standardization for evaluating transplant
centers. *Journal of Hospital Administration*, 8(1), 9-14.
